name: vllm.cpp
notable_features: Ports vLLM's serving core - continuous batching, block-paged KV, the V1 scheduler, automatic prefix caching, speculative decoding - into from-scratch C++20 with no Python and no PyTorch at inference time
Ships SGLang's scheduling ideas as documented toggles: RadixAttention, LPM cache-aware admission, jump-forward decoding
Does NOT use ggml: it reads GGUF and follows llama.cpp's C ABI style but has its own portable vt:: tensor runtime
Versioned flat C ABI (include/vllm.h, VLLM_ABI_VERSION) with append-only fields, so embedders can rely on it
Claims token-for-token identical output to vLLM as its correctness gate, plus prebuilt CPU/CUDA/Vulkan/Metal/MLX release archives
hardware_caveats: Under heavy development by its own README: internals, CLI flags and server behaviour can change between commits, so tracking main means expecting breakage
Independent and unofficial - not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by the vLLM project, the PyTorch Foundation or the Linux Foundation
Kernel coverage is uneven by format: TQ1_0/TQ2_0 GGUF loading is unsupported even though Vulkan has ternary matmul and fused-MoE kernels for them
AMD path is brand new: EXL3 gained a native ROCm path validated only on gfx1151 with no CPU fallbacks; discrete AMD validation and competitive performance are explicitly unmeasured

Several architectures are token-gated but not speed-gated (GLM-5.3's real 201.83 GiB artifact has never completed a load), and multimodal HTTP input has CPU tests with synthetic weights with real-checkpoint parity unverified

Its performance claims are self-reported by the project against its own vLLM oracle on one GB10 machine; the concurrency sweep from c2 to c32 is inside the stated 0.5% noise band, and one headline comparison is marked SUPERSEDED in its own docs
best_for: Deploying a single binary with no Python runtime where vLLM-equivalent scheduling is still wanted
Reproducing vLLM scheduling semantics token-for-token outside the PyTorch ecosystem
Constraints where a 66 MiB binary versus a multi-gigabyte Python install is the deciding factor
avoid_for: Production deployments that need a stable API surface - the project says so itself
AMD GPUs, where the path exists but is essentially unvalidated
Any claim of measured superiority over vLLM: the published comparison is one machine, one model, self-measured, and mostly inside its own noise band
notes: Benchmark numbers in the README (Qwen3.6-27B NVFP4 on NVIDIA GB10: 86.05 tok/s at c1 rising to 1095.01 tok/s at c32 vs vLLM's 82.32 to 1076.25; 45.45 vs 41.94 tok/s on Qwen3-8B MXFP4) are vendor self-reported and were NOT independently reproduced here. Recorded for traceability only; no benchmark record was created because this slice does not own benchmarks/.
